query_text: Why does my cat kick its toys when playing with them?

message.content:
Your cat kicks its toys due to natural instincts inherited from their wild ancestors. This behavior, often called "bunny kicking," serves several purposes:

## Play Hunting Practice

Even well-fed house cats retain strong hunting instincts. Kittens learn to bunny kick during early play with their mothers and littermates, mimicking how they would capture and subdue prey in the wild. When your cat grabs a toy with their front paws and kicks rapidly with their hind legs, they're practicing the same technique wild cats use to disembowel or disable prey.

## Self-Defense Skills

Bunny kicking is also an important defensive maneuver. If a cat is on their back during a real fight, they can use all four sets of claws plus their teeth to inflict maximum damage on an opponent while protecting their vulnerable belly. Kicking toys helps keep these defensive skills sharp.

## Play Fighting and Exercise

This behavior provides full-body exercise, engaging your cat's core muscles, hind leg strength, and cardiovascular system. It's a natural way for cats to burn energy and relieve stress through physical activity.

## Overstimulation Release

Sometimes bunny kicking indicates your cat is getting overstimulated during play. It's their way of saying the excitement is getting a bit too intense.

## How to Channel This Behavior Safely

Since this is normal feline behavior, it's best to provide appropriate outlets rather than try to stop it. **Kicker toys**—oblong, often catnip-filled plush toys designed to withstand vigorous kicking—are ideal. Avoid letting your cat practice this behavior on your arm, as those powerful back legs can cause painful scratches. Regular interactive play with wand toys can also help burn off excess energy before it turns into overly enthusiastic kicking.
